sections.h2: Which Lawrence County offices deal with a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Lawrence County government sits in Louisa, and the offices that matter to a property owner are all within a few doors of each other at the courthouse area on Main Cross Street. Each one handles a different stage of the tax year.

  • Property Valuation Administrator (PVA): 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa, KY 41230. The PVA sets the assessed value and takes homestead applications.
  • Sheriff: 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa. Phone (606) 638-4368. The sheriff collects the bill.
  • County Clerk: runs the appeals board paperwork and, after April, the sale of unpaid bills. The clerk's site posts the current delinquent list.
  • County Attorney: mails the warning letters to owners whose bills have moved to the clerk.

For a specific parcel, ask the sheriff for the bill and the PVA for the assessment. The rate varies by taxing district, so a countywide figure can mislead.

sections.h2: What is Lawrence County like for a property owner?
sections.html:
Lawrence County was formed in 1821 from parts of Floyd and Greenup counties and has had four courthouses over the years. Louisa is the only city and the county seat. The county runs along the Big Sandy River in the east, where a quarter-mile concrete T-bridge carries traffic between Louisa and Fort Gay, West Virginia. Yatesville Lake, a reservoir of about 2,300 acres opened in 1992 and managed by the Army Corps of Engineers, gives the county flood control and boating. Alcohol sales are limited to Louisa city limits.

  • Population: 15,765 in the July 2025 estimate, down 3.2 percent from the April 2020 base. The land area is about 416 square miles, or 39 people per square mile.
  • Housing: 7,737 units and 6,342 households, with 77.8 percent owned by their occupants.
  • Middle home value: $111,700. Owners with a mortgage pay about $1,216 a month in owner costs, and those without pay $386.
  • Income: $46,772 for the median household, with 23.4 percent of people in poverty.
  • Work: 207 employer establishments with 2,950 jobs in 2023, a 5.9 percent rise over 2022, and a 30.1 minute average commute.

sections.h2: When is the bill due, and what do late payments cost?
sections.html:
Value is set on January 1 and the tax for that year is owed by the end of December, payable to the sheriff. KRS 134.015 puts numbers on the calendar.

  • Full payment by November 1 earns a 2 percent discount.
  • November 2 through December 31 is the printed amount.
  • January adds a 5 percent penalty.
  • After January 31 the penalty is 10 percent.

The Department of Revenue explains that the sheriff also adds a 10 percent fee after January, so the practical total from February 1 is about 21 percent plus commission. When collections start after November 1, the state uses an alternative schedule that gives owners 30 days for each stage of the cycle. Lawrence County bills for oil and gas also exist, and the clerk has noted that its most recent sale left out the 2023 oil and gas bills, so ask the sheriff whether such a bill sits against a parcel.

sections.h2: How do Lawrence County owners appeal an assessment?
sections.html:
The first move is a conference with the PVA or a deputy at the courthouse, and an appeal to the board cannot be filed without one. The tax roll is open for inspection for thirteen days beginning the first Monday in May, with Saturdays included. The clerk receives the appeal, and it is due by the close of business on the workday after the inspection period ends.

The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days later and decides on evidence only. Owners bring facts such as descriptions of the land and buildings, insurance papers, construction costs and listings of comparable sales. The board must explain in writing any change it makes, and owners may record the hearing on audio. Paid representatives must come from the categories listed in KRS 133.120, which include attorneys, accountants, licensed brokers and appraisers. An owner who skips the local board loses access to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

sections.h2: Do older or disabled Lawrence County owners get a tax break?
sections.html:
Yes. The homestead exemption subtracts $49,100 from the assessment for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years, so a $150,000 home would be taxed as $100,900. It is open to owners who are 65 or older and to owners classified as totally disabled. In Lawrence County 19.9 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 17.5 percent of those under 65 report a disability, so the exemption applies to a large share of households.

Applications go to the PVA at the courthouse. Proof of age can be a birth certificate, driver's license or passport. Disability claims require a federal or retirement system classification of total disability and payments throughout the assessment period, and most are renewed each year. Veterans with a service connected disability and owners found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or the state retirement systems do not have to renew.

sections.h2: How does the Lawrence County Clerk sell unpaid tax bills?
sections.html:
After the sheriff's April 15 cutoff, unpaid bills go to the clerk as certificates of delinquency, and interest of 1 percent a month starts. The county attorney mails notices, and the clerk advertises the list before the sale. At the sale a third party can buy the lien, and the owner then pays that buyer instead. The Lawrence County Clerk's website lays out how its draft-style sale works, which also tells an owner how much the buyer may be paying.

Lawrence County Clerk delinquent tax sale rules (lawrencekyclerk.com, delinquent taxes page)
ItemRule
RegistrationAt least 10 business days before the sale
Deposit$10 per bill, capped at $250, not refundable
Prior year certificatesSeparate list due 10 business days before the sale
Bidders per entityOne potential purchaser
Order of purchaseRandom drawing, lowest number picks first, in rounds
PaymentCash, certified check, money order or company check
RefundsNone after the sale

The lien on the land from delinquent taxes lasts eleven years under KRS 134.015, no matter who owns the property.

sections.h2: What should a Lawrence County seller handle before listing?
sections.html:
• Ask the sheriff at (606) 638-4368 for the current bill and any earlier unpaid year.
  • Check the clerk's delinquent list to see whether a certificate already exists on the parcel.
  • If you hold the homestead exemption, ask the PVA how it is treated after a sale.
  • Compare your assessment with the sales of similar houses before the May inspection window opens, in case a dispute is worth filing.
  • Agree on the split of the current bill in the sales contract.

A seller who would rather not repair or show the house can ask for a direct offer. Taxes still come out of the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Lawrence County?
faqs.a: The Lawrence County Sheriff collects it at 122 Main Cross Street in Louisa. Call (606) 638-4368 to confirm the amount and the payment methods before you go.

faqs.q: What is the early payment discount in Lawrence County?
faqs.a: Two percent, if the bill is paid in full by November 1. KRS 134.015 sets that discount, and the printed amount applies from November 2 through December 31.

faqs.q: What is the first step to dispute a Lawrence County assessment?
faqs.a: Meet with the PVA or a deputy. The local board of assessment appeals will not hear an owner who has not had that conference first.

faqs.q: How much does the homestead exemption remove from the assessment?
faqs.a: It removes $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. Owners must be 65 or older or classified as totally disabled, and the PVA takes the application.

faqs.q: Can a third party buy my unpaid Lawrence County tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. If a certificate of delinquency is unpaid at the clerk's sale, a registered third party purchaser can buy the lien, and the owner then pays that buyer.
